questions.question: Why does changing a copied object sometimes change the original? Explain reference, shallow copy and deep copy.
questions.answer: Objects are reference values: the variable holds a pointer, not the data. const b = a copies the pointer, so a and b are the same object and any write through either is visible through both. A shallow copy — { ...a } or Object.assign({}, a) — creates a new outer object but copies the nested values as references, so a nested object or array is still shared: mutating copy.address changes a.address. A deep copy recursively clones every level. structuredClone(obj) is the built-in that handles nested objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set and cycles; JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) also deep-clones but only for plain JSON data, losing Dates, undefined, functions and Map/Set. Primitives (string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint) are copied by value, so they never have this problem.
key_points: Object variables hold references; `=` aliases the object
Spread and Object.assign are shallow — nested values stay shared
structuredClone is the deep copy tool; JSON clone is lossy
Primitives copy by value, objects copy by reference

questions.answer:
It prints true, then 'fr'.

Object.assign(target, ...sources) mutates and returns target. Because the first argument here is defaults, settings and defaults are literally the same object — settings === defaults is true. The spread-looking syntax does not create a copy. The safe form is Object.assign({}, defaults, overrides).

The second line shows shallowness: assign copied nested by reference, so settings.nested and defaults.nested are one object. Writing lang through settings is visible through defaults. Object.assign({}, defaults, overrides) would fix the top-level aliasing but still share nested; use structuredClone or spread at each level you intend to change.
key_points: Object.assign mutates the first argument and returns it
Use Object.assign({}, defaults, overrides) to avoid mutating defaults
The copy is shallow — nested objects are shared
Fix nested sharing with structuredClone or per-level spreads

questions.answer:
It prints { when: '2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z', count: null }, then false.

JSON only knows objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Date has a toJSON method, so it is serialized to an ISO string and never revived as a Date. NaN and Infinity are not valid JSON numbers, so JSON.stringify writes null. undefined values (and functions and symbols) are dropped entirely, which is why tag is missing rather than null. Map and Set become {}, BigInt throws TypeError, and circular references throw.

The clone is fine for plain data but silently changes types — which is dangerous if code later calls clone.when.getFullYear(). Use structuredClone(original) to keep Date, Map, Set and undefined values.
key_points: Date becomes an ISO string, not a Date
NaN and Infinity become null
undefined, functions and symbols are dropped
Map/Set become {}, BigInt and cycles throw
structuredClone preserves types

questions.question: Compare Object.freeze and Object.seal. What exactly do they prevent, and why is neither a deep protection?
questions.answer:
Object.freeze makes every own property non-writable and non-configurable and prevents adding new ones — the object is effectively read-only. Object.seal prevents adding and deleting properties but leaves existing values writable. Both return the same object, and both are shallow: they only change the property descriptors of the object you pass. A nested object is a separate object, so its properties stay writable unless you freeze it too.

Failure behaviour depends on strictness. In sloppy mode, writes and deletes fail silently; in strict mode or an ES module, assignment to a frozen property or deletion of a sealed one throws TypeError. After freezing, Object.isFrozen(obj) is true, and Object.isSealed is also true for a frozen object (freeze is a stronger seal). Freeze is a guard against accidental mutation, not a security boundary — code can still replace nested values and the prototype chain is untouched.
key_points: freeze = no add, no edit, no delete (non-writable + non-configurable)
seal = no add, no delete, but values stay writable
Both are shallow — nested objects need their own freeze
Sloppy mode fails silently; strict/modules throw TypeError
A frozen object is also sealed

questions.answer:
It prints name and role, then [ 'name' ].

for...in walks the entire prototype chain and includes inherited enumerable properties, so role from proto shows up even though user never defined it. Object.keys only returns own enumerable properties, which is why it shows just name. Object.hasOwn(user, "role") is false while "role" in user is true — `in` also walks the chain.

Fix: iterate with Object.keys(user), Object.entries(user) or Object.values(user), or guard inside the loop with if (Object.hasOwn(user, key)) continue. Never use for...in on plain data objects; it also picks up any library that adds enumerable properties to Object.prototype. hasOwnProperty works too, but fails on Object.create(null) objects, so Object.hasOwn is the safer modern choice.
key_points: for...in includes inherited enumerable properties
Object.keys returns own enumerable string keys only
`in` walks the prototype chain; Object.hasOwn does not
Prefer Object.keys/entries or guard with Object.hasOwn
